definition: Re-roofing replaces a worn roof covering with a new underlayment-and-cover system once the existing roof reaches the end of its service life by age or condition, renewing the entire weatherproof surface rather than patching isolated damage. It is the umbrella term that, per ARMA and the IRC R908 reroofing section, covers both a full tear-off replacement and a recover (overlay) over a single sound layer. It applies once the roof crosses the replacement threshold rather than when a single detail has failed.

signs: A roof at or past its material lifespan signals re-roofing, because 3-tab asphalt lasts 20 years and architectural asphalt 30 years, with actual life varying up to 40% with climate and maintenance, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart and the NRCA.

An asphalt roof past 20 years, or 15 on the coast, crosses the age rule that favors re-roofing, because a localized repair stays the more economical path only while the roof stays under 10 to 15 years old, per WeatherShield and Home Depot cost data.

Damage across more than 25–30% of the roof area crosses the contractor-consensus 25% rule, the threshold above which a full re-roof costs less than continued spot repair, per RapidRestore and MyQuoteIQ guidance.

A repair quote approaching 50% of replacement cost crosses the contractor-consensus 50% rule, the point at which re-roofing returns more value than a repair, per WeatherShield and Home Depot guidance.
Three or more repairs in 2 years crosses the contractor-consensus 3-repairs rule, the signal of a systemic failure rather than an isolated defect, per WeatherShield guidance.

Granule loss with sandy grit in gutters and a bald asphalt mat indicates shingles nearing end of life, and granule loss exceeding 30% of the surface is the common rule-of-thumb for beyond repair, per GAF.
A spongy or sagging roof deck indicates moisture-rotted sheathing or framing, a structural condition that a full tear-off exposes for repair, per GAF inspection guidance.
Daylight seen through the roof deck from inside the attic indicates holes in the decking and shingles, a sign that points toward re-roofing rather than a patch, per This Old House.
selectionCriteria: Verify New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, with the 13VH registration number shown on the contract and any advertisement per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 — it is a registration, not a roofing license, because New Jersey issues no roofing license.
Confirm at least $500,000 per-occurrence commercial general liability coverage required of a registered NJ HIC under N.J.S.A. 56:8-142, verified by a current certificate of insurance.
Require a written contract for any job over $500 under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2, with scope, total price, and start and completion dates set in writing before work begins.

Require an itemized written estimate that lists tear-off, deck repair, ice barrier, underlayment, the cover, disposal, and the permit when one is triggered, so disposal and code-required ice-and-water shield are not silently excluded.

Confirm a documented roof and deck assessment that tests the re-roofing decision against the 25% area rule, the 50% cost rule, the age rule at 20 years (15 coastal), and the 3-repairs-in-2-years rule before quoting, per WeatherShield and RapidRestore decision guidance.
Ask for local Essex County references and a written workmanship warranty on the labor that is separate from the manufacturer material warranty on the product.

technicalFacts.fact: Re-roofing is the umbrella term for recovering OR replacing an existing roof covering, so it covers both a full tear-off replacement and a recover over a single sound layer.
technicalFacts.source: ARMA; ICC IRC R908 reroofing section

technicalFacts.fact: A full tear-off strips the covering to the deck, which provides the opportunity to inspect the roof deck, repair damage, and improve deck attachment to the structure, while a recover hides deck rot and water damage a tear-off would catch.

A roof-over (recover) is prohibited where the existing roof is water-soaked or deteriorated, where the existing covering is wood shake, slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile, or where two or more applications already exist (no third layer).

A complete tear-off and re-roof of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance requiring no construction permit, while a structural change to rafters or trusses still triggers a permit.
On a commercial building a re-roof requires a permit, because the ordinary-maintenance exemption covers only repair of up to 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period.
A recover over a single sound asphalt layer traps heat that industry estimates cut shingle service life by roughly 20–30%, so a 25-year shingle may deliver only about 17–20 years over an overlay.

A second overlay layer adds roughly 2 to 4.5 lb per square foot of dead load (thousands of extra pounds across deck, rafters, and walls), telegraphs the old shingle profile, and forces a costlier future double tear-off.
Material lifespans differ sharply: 3-tab asphalt lasts 20 years, architectural asphalt 30 years, metal 40 to 80 years, and slate 60 to 150 years, with premium slate commonly 100-plus years.
technicalFacts.source: InterNACHI life-expectancy chart; National Slate Association

technicalFacts.fact: An ice barrier is installed from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line.

A low-slope roof needs at least ¼ inch per foot of slope to drain, with ponding water remaining more than 48 hours counted as a defect; commercial EPDM lasts 15–25 years, TPO 7–20 years, and modified bitumen 20 years.
technicalFacts.source: NRCA and ARMA; InterNACHI life-expectancy chart

technicalFacts.fact: Newark crosses the 32°F freezing point repeatedly through winter with an average January low near 25.5°F, driving freeze-thaw stress on sealants and fasteners.

Installing the new cover to manufacturer specification preserves the manufacturer material warranty that covers factory defects, which is separate from the contractor's written workmanship warranty on the labor.
A new asphalt roof recoups roughly 60 to 68% of project cost at resale, and 8 of the top 10 highest-ROI remodels are exterior replacement projects.
technicalFacts.source: Zillow resale analysis; Zonda Cost vs Value report

technicalFacts.fact: Replacement accounts for 79.2% of US roofing installations in 2025, and asphalt shingles cover roughly 73% of US residential roofs.

defabToKill.issue: "Three-tab asphalt shingles typically need re-roofing at 18-22 years, while architectural shingles last 22-28 years." — invented age ranges not in gold.
defabToKill.fix: Use the gold/InterNACHI lifespans: 3-tab asphalt lasts 20 years and architectural asphalt 30 years, with actual life varying up to 40% with climate and maintenance, per the InterNACHI chart and the NRCA.

defabToKill.issue: "south-facing slopes in open areas like Livingston age faster than shaded north-facing slopes in tree-covered Maplewood" and "Cedar shake roofs ... typically need replacement at 25-30 years in New Jersey, particularly in low-lying areas near the Passaic River" — invented microclimate/cedar age claims with no source.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the invented per-town aging and cedar-age numbers. Frame aging generally via the gold: actual asphalt life varies up to 40% with climate, install, and maintenance, per the NRCA. Do not assert a cedar-shake NJ lifespan that the gold does not carry.

defabToKill.issue: "we see granule loss accelerate after hailstorms, which occur 2-4 times annually in the Newark metropolitan area" — invented unsourced hail-frequency climate figure.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the '2-4 times annually' hail figure (no NOAA source). State the gold granule-loss sign: granule loss with sandy grit in gutters and a bald asphalt mat indicates shingles nearing end of life, with loss exceeding 30% of the surface the rule-of-thumb for beyond repair, per GAF.

defabToKill.issue: "In New Jersey, where we average 49 inches of annual rainfall, a roof that cannot handle routine precipitation..." — unsourced climate figure not attributable to NOAA in the fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the '49 inches' rainfall figure. Frame recurring leaks via the gold: three or more repairs in 2 years crosses the contractor-consensus 3-repairs rule, the signal of systemic failure rather than an isolated defect, per WeatherShield.

defabToKill.issue: "Asphalt shingle re-roofing ... ranges from $6,500 (overlay with three-tab shingles) to $15,000 (tear-off with architectural shingles). Metal re-roofing runs $12,000-$22,000, while slate or tile re-roofing ... can reach $25,000-$45,000." — invented flat whole-roof totals not in gold.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with gold figures: NJ re-roofing of a typical home costs $10,000–$25,000 per HomeAdvisor and Modernize NJ, with material per-sf rates of $6.50–$11.00 architectural asphalt and $9.00–$16.00 metal per Josten Roofing NJ pricing and $10–$30 slate per NJ roofing guides.

defabToKill.issue: "Material costs represent roughly 40% of the total, with labor at 50% and permits, disposal, and overhead at 10%." — invented cost-split percentages not in gold.
defabToKill.fix: Use the gold labor share: labor accounts for roughly 60–70% of an asphalt-install total, per HomeGuide and Integrity Home Exteriors. Do not assert a 40/50/10 split.

defabToKill.issue: "NJ labor rates ... run higher than the national average due to licensing requirements" — implies a NJ roofing license that does not exist.
defabToKill.fix: Reframe to registration, not a license: NJ ranges sit 10–40% above national figures because of higher labor and stricter NJ code, per HomeGuide and Integrity Home Exteriors; contractors are registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractors, not licensed (NJ issues no roofing license).

defabToKill.issue: "These steep roofs cost 20-30% more than standard 4/12 to 6/12 pitches" and "Off-season projects often receive 5-10% better pricing" — invented percentage cost adjustments with no source.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the 20–30% pitch surcharge and the 5–10% off-season discount (unsourced). Frame cost drivers qualitatively via gold: material drives per-sf cost and tear-off adds cost over a recover, per Josten Roofing and HomeGuide; do not assign unsourced percentages.

defabToKill.issue: "Get three written estimates from NJ Home Improvement Contractor (HIC) registered companies." — correct on registration but pair with the specific statutory anchor it omits.
defabToKill.fix: Keep the registered-HIC framing and anchor it: verify NJ HIC registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136 (13VH number per 56:8-144) and a written contract for any job over $500 under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2.

defabToKill.issue: "Every re-roofing project in New Jersey requires a municipal building permit. Essex County towns process these in 3-10 business days..." — wrong; contradicts the ordinary-maintenance no-permit rule and invents a processing window.
defabToKill.fix: Correct via gold: a complete re-roof of the covering on a detached one- and two-family home is ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires NO construction permit; a commercial re-roof or a structural change does require a permit. Drop the invented 3-10 day processing figure.

defabToKill.issue: "Summer's extreme heat can affect adhesive activation on shingles, while winter installations below 40 degrees compromise the self-sealing strip. Emergency re-roofing accommodates any season with cold-weather adhesive and heat guns..." — unsourced installation-temperature/season claims.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the unsourced 40-degree threshold and season claims. If climate is mentioned, use the sourced fact: Newark crosses 32°F repeatedly in winter (average January low near 25.5°F), driving freeze-thaw stress, per NOAA 1991–2020 normals at EWR.

defabToKill.issue: "Crews arrive at 7:00-7:30 AM..." and "Most standard Essex County homes complete re-roofing in 1-3 days. Complex homes ... may require an additional day." — invented timeline/scheduling specifics not in gold.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the invented arrival time and 1–3 day duration. The gold gives no project-day timeline; describe the process via the gold processSteps (threshold and deck assessment, written estimate and material selection, permits, tear-off and deck repair, ice barrier/underlayment/cover install, verification/cleanup/warranty) without asserting a day count.

defabToKill.issue: "For most Essex County homes with a single layer in reasonable condition, overlay provides excellent value." — presents a recover as a free win without the gold/fact-pack trade-offs.
defabToKill.fix: Present overlay honestly per the fact pack: a recover skips tear-off labor and disposal (about 20–25% / $2,000–$5,000 less, national figures) but hides deck rot a tear-off catches, traps heat that cuts shingle life ~20–30%, telegraphs the old profile, adds thousands of pounds of dead load, and is prohibited under N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 over a deteriorated deck, wood shake/slate/clay/cement/asbestos-cement tile, or two existing layers.

parentDebtToAvoid: Parent gold commercial block names 'Firestone, Carlisle, and Johns Manville membrane systems' — do NOT reproduce the brand-roster line; describe EPDM/TPO/modified-bitumen membrane generically.
Parent gold credentialsHighlight carries 'NJ HIC Licensed' — use 'registered NJ HIC' / 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor'; never 'licensed', because NJ issues no roofing license.

Never present GAF/CertainTeed/Owens Corning as NQR certifications or partnerships (no Master Elite, SELECT ShingleMaster, Preferred, Golden Pledge, '~2% qualify'); name them only as external warranty/install guidance, and explain warranty as two parts — manufacturer material warranty (factory defects, preserved when installed to manufacturer spec) plus the contractor's written workmanship warranty (labor).
Do not invent volume claims (e.g., 'hundreds of roofs'); NQR is a registered NJ HIC serving Essex County with no stated counts.

articleAngles.signs: Re-roofing is signaled by the roof crossing a replacement threshold rather than a single failed detail — define it via the contractor-consensus rules and end-of-life indicators: a roof at or past its material lifespan (3-tab 20 yrs, architectural 30 yrs per InterNACHI/NRCA), damage across more than 25–30% of the area, a repair quote approaching 50% of replacement cost, three or more repairs in 2 years, granule loss with bald mat, a spongy/sagging deck, or attic daylight.
articleAngles.costGuide: There IS a real whole-job total: re-roofing a typical NJ home costs $10,000–$25,000 per HomeAdvisor and Modernize NJ, against a 2025 national average near $10,000–$11,000; material then drives per-sf cost ($6.50–$11.00 architectural asphalt, $9.00–$16.00 metal per Josten Roofing NJ; $10–$30 slate), tear-off adds $1–$3/sf for shingles ($2–$5 slate/tile per HomeGuide), labor is roughly 60–70% of the total, and NJ runs 10–40% above national.
articleAngles.decision: The single most important thing to understand is that re-roofing is the umbrella term covering both a full tear-off replacement and a recover (overlay) over one sound layer, and that the tear-off-vs-overlay choice is constrained by code, not just budget: an overlay is prohibited under N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 / IRC R908.3.1.1 where the deck is water-soaked or deteriorated, the existing covering is wood shake/slate/clay/cement/asbestos-cement tile, or two layers already exist — and even when allowed, the ~20–25% overlay savings come with hidden deck rot, a ~20–30% shingle-life haircut, a telegraphed profile, added dead load, and a costlier future double tear-off.
